summary.text: A virus is a submicroscopic infectious agent that makes copies of itself only inside the living cells of an organism.
Viruses infect all life forms, from animals and plants to bacteria and archaea, and they are the most numerous type of biological entity.
Away from a cell, a virus is a particle of DNA or RNA inside a protein coat, and in some cases an outer envelope of lipids.

facts.label: First one found
facts.value: The tobacco mosaic virus, in the 1890s

facts.label: Size of virions
facts.value: Most are one-hundredth the size of most bacteria

facts.label: How they spread
facts.value: Insect vectors, coughs and sneezes, food, water, sexual contact

items.prompt: A virus particle sits on a kitchen counter, far from any living cell. What can it do there?

options.label: Multiply slowly using moisture from the counter
Feed on crumbs and grow into a larger particle
Stay intact but make no copies, since copying needs a living cell
Split in two the way a bacterium does

items.explain: A virus replicates only inside living cells. Outside them it exists as an independent particle.

items.prompt: In a virion, what directly wraps around the genetic material to protect it?

options.label: A protein coat
An outer envelope of lipids
A cell wall made of sugars
A second set of spare RNA copies

items.explain: The protein coat, the capsid, surrounds and protects the genetic material. A lipid envelope, when present, lies outside.

items.prompt: One virus infects only two or three species. Another infects dozens. How are the two described by the variety of cells they can infect?

options.label: The first has a broad range and the second a narrow one
Both are the same, since both infect animals
Viruses have no measure of this kind
The first has a narrow range and the second a broad one

items.explain: The variety of host cells a virus can infect is its host range: narrow for a few species, broad for many.

items.prompt: A person is vaccinated against one specific virus. What does the vaccine do for them?

options.label: It gives lasting protection against every virus at once
It triggers an immune response that gives artificial immunity to that infection
It destroys virus particles directly, like an antiviral drug
It swaps their immune system for an artificial one

items.explain: Immune responses can be produced by vaccines, which confer artificially acquired immunity to the specific viral infection.

items.prompt: The immune system usually clears a viral infection in animals. Why do some, such as HIV, linger for years?

options.label: Their particles are too big for immune cells to reach
The immune system never responds to any virus at all
These viruses evade the immune response and cause chronic infections
Antiviral drugs keep them from ever leaving the body

items.explain: Viral infections usually provoke an immune response that eliminates the virus, but some viruses evade it.

items.prompt: Bones and shells fossilise, yet viruses leave nothing in rock. How can researchers still trace ancient viruses?

options.label: With molecular techniques and viral genes that joined hosts' germlines
By digging up virus fossils in very old rock layers
By counting the virions that survive in old ice
By measuring how large virions are today

items.explain: Viruses do not form fossils, so molecular techniques infer their origins. Viral genetic material integrated into host germlines is passed down and lets paleovirologists trace ancient viruses.
